summary: Learners aged 9–11 practise the procedural skill of reading weather maps: decoding map symbols (temperature, precipitation, wind), extracting specific values from data tables and graphs, spotting trends across a time series, and using a pattern to make a justified, probabilistic prediction. Teach the symbol key explicitly first, then move from single-map reading to trend-spotting across a series, then to predict-then-check with authentic maps and the class's own weather-diary data.
misconceptions: A weather map shows the weather everywhere all the time — it is a snapshot/forecast for a moment or period
A single data point shows a trend — trends need a series of readings
Predictions from data are certainties — they are probabilities read from patterns
All symbols are self-evident — many (fronts, wind barbs, pressure) must be decoded from a key
Higher numbers always mean 'worse' weather — units and what is measured matter

activities.title: Crack the code: decode a real weather map
steps: Study a labelled weather map showing temperature figures, weather icons (e.g. sun, cloud, rain), wind symbols (arrows or barbs), and front/pressure symbols.

Use the actual map’s key to decode temperature, precipitation, fronts, pressure and wind. State wind direction and speed only as encoded by that key, including any arrow length, colour, label or barb markings.

Name wind by the direction it comes from. Check the map’s key to decide whether a wind arrow points toward its destination or a staff extends toward its origin, and translate that symbol into the correct from-direction.
Explain, for a named front or pressure symbol, what weather it tends to bring.
activities.insight: A weather map is a decodable instrument, not decoration: many symbols (fronts, wind barbs, pressure) must be read from a key rather than guessed, and a map is a snapshot/forecast for a moment or period, not the weather everywhere all the time.

activities.title: Read the data and name the trend
steps: Read a time-series table or graph of weather data (e.g. temperature or rainfall over a week, month or season).
Extract specific values when asked: the highest temperature, which day was wettest, the value on a named day.
Track a finger from each data point to the labelled axis and check the units before reporting a value.
Look across ALL the data points and name the trend (e.g. temperatures rising through the week, rainfall decreasing, pressure falling).
activities.insight: A trend requires a series of readings — a single data point is not a pattern — and correct reading depends on checking the axis scale and units, since higher numbers do not automatically mean 'worse' weather.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: forecast tomorrow from the pattern
steps: Read the trend across the data series for a named place.
Commit to a prediction for tomorrow's (or the next period's) conditions, explicitly grounding it in the observed pattern.
Reveal or record the actual outcome and compare it with the prediction.
Reflect on matches and mismatches, articulating that a forecast is a probability read from a pattern, not a guarantee.
activities.insight: A data-based prediction is a probability read from a pattern — it should be justified by the trend and may still turn out wrong; this is the payoff of interpreting the map and data.

activities.title: Symbol- and graph-reading checks (companion assessment)
steps: Answer targeted questions: 'What does this symbol mean?', 'What pattern does this graph show?', and 'Predict from this data.'
Select or state the correct value read from a specific graph or table.
Choose or state a prediction that follows from the shown trend and justify the choice.
activities.insight: Symbol meaning, pattern identification, and data-based prediction can each be checked directly, surfacing whether the learner can apply the interpretation procedure.

checkQuestion: Give the child a real weather map (symbols for sun, rain, wind arrows and temperatures) and a table or graph of a week's weather data. Ask them to tell you tomorrow's likely conditions for a named place, read off specific values (the highest temperature, which day was wettest) and say what pattern the data shows — then watch how they read the symbols and use the data. Don't ask them to define the symbols; watch them use them.
checkAnswer: Reads the symbols correctly (temperature figures, rain/sun icons, wind arrows for direction and often strength), extracts specific values from the table/graph, identifies a trend (e.g. temperatures rising through the week, a front approaching) and uses the pattern to make a reasonable prediction for the named place.
